name: Thiruvalleeswarar Temple, Padi
deity: Shiva as Thiruvalleeswarar (Valithayanathar), with the goddess Jagadambika
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Thondai country sung in the Tevaram (7th-century hymns); structural temple of the Chola period with later additions
summary: Thiruvalleeswarar at Padi is the Tiruvalithayam of the Tevaram, a Thondai Nadu shrine where a sage reborn as a bird is said to have found the Lord beneath a tree, and where Brihaspati, the planet Jupiter, was freed from a curse — the reason Chennai honours it as a Guru sthalam.

sections.history: Padi, now a north-western neighbourhood of Chennai, holds one of the old Shaiva shrines of the Thondai country. In the Tevaram hymns the place is Tiruvalithayam, praised by Thirugnana Sambandar, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam, one of the temples sung by the saints. Inscriptions and the fabric of the sanctum place the structural temple in the Chola age, around the eleventh century, with later hands enlarging it; tradition remembers damage in the wars of medieval times and a careful restoration. The place name is read from the story of a sage reborn as a bird, and through the centuries the shrine has stayed in worship, tended today by the state endowments department.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east, entered beneath a three-tiered gopuram that opens onto a courtyard with the flagstaff and the seated Nandi before the Lord. The east-facing sanctum of Thiruvalleeswarar, who is worshipped as a Shiva linga, is crowned by a vimana in the apsidal gajaprishta form, shaped like the curve of an elephant's back, an older and distinctive profile among the region's temples. The goddess Jagadambika is honoured in her own south-facing shrine beside the sanctum. In the courtyard stands a shrine to Guru, the planet Jupiter, for which the temple is widely known, and the sacred tree is the padiri; the temple tank is remembered as the Bharadwaja Theertham.
sections.legends: Two stories give the temple its name and its fame. In the first, the sage Bharadwaja, born in the body of a small bird the Tamil call valiyan, wandered the holy places grieving his lowly birth, and at this spot found a Shiva linga beneath a kondrai tree and worshipped it; the Lord appeared and made him the leader of the birds, and from the bird the place became Valithayam and the Lord Valithayanathar. The second is the story most devotees come for: Brihaspati, the planet Jupiter and preceptor of the gods, fell under a curse, and on the counsel of the sage Markandeya he bathed in the temple tank and worshipped here, and was freed. From this the shrine is counted among the Guru parihara sthalams, the places that soften the influence of Jupiter, and Chennai honours it as its Guru temple.
sections.festivals: The temple's foremost festival is the Chithirai Brahmotsavam in April or May, when the deities are drawn in procession through the streets of Padi. Because the shrine is a Guru sthalam, the transits of Jupiter — the Guru Peyarchi days — draw large gatherings, and Thursdays, the day of Guru, are kept with special worship through the year. Thai Krithikai in January or February, Maha Shivaratri, and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Padi sits amid the mills and busy roads of northern Chennai, yet within the walls the temple keeps an older stillness. Enter beneath the eastern gopuram, pause at the Nandi and the flagstaff, and come to the sanctum of Thiruvalleeswarar beneath its curved apsidal tower before turning to the goddess Jagadambika in her shrine. Many visitors come above all for Guru, standing before the shrine of Jupiter to pray for learning and for relief from the planet's hard aspects, and Thursdays bring the largest crowds. It is an easy shrine to reach within the city and an unhurried one to pray in.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; local listings give roughly 6:30 a.m. to noon and 4:30 to 8:30 p.m. Confirm timings locally, especially on Thursdays and festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Padi lies in north-western Chennai, off Avadi Road near the TVS and MTC junctions; the temple is a short walk from the Padi Lucas-TVS bus stop. Frequent city buses serve the area, and Chennai's suburban rail and the Chennai Central and airport are within the metropolitan reach by road.
